newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland counts down fearfully to more parades.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland counts down fearfully to more parades.

text.p: Still reeling from nightly violence that followed one Orange Order parade, Northern Ireland began counting down on Wednesday to equally charged marches at the weekend climax of the Protestant "marching season".

A radical IRA splinter group, the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA), threatened to attack members of the Orange Order if they insisted on carrying out plans to march down the Lower Ormeau Road in Belfast on Saturday morning.
"If any more Loyalist marches are forced through Nationalist communities we will move from our position of defence and retaliation," an INLA statement said.
"Those within the Loyalist orders, organisations and groups deemed to be responsible for the misery heaped upon our communities will be made accountable," it said.

A Catholic residents' group in Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city, called in a statement for a huge rally to protest against the holding of a march by the Apprentice Boys, another Protestant organisation, on the same day. The Bogside residents group said the protest was intended to be peaceful but made clear that it wanted the parade stopped.
The 12th of July marks the anniversary of a 1690 Protestant battle victory over an invading Catholic King and is seen by Catholics as an anachronistic display of triumphalism.

The INLA claimed responsibility for several of the shooting attacks on British troops and police which have been staged nightly since Sunday's march. Two police officers have been injured but no one has been killed.

The statement was issued hours after masked gunmen hijacked a Belfast-bound train at the border town of Newry and set a carriage ablaze in sporadic violence that flared across the province, albeit on a lower scale than on previous days.

Sections of a key highway were blocked by blazing cars hijacked by angry Catholic youths and security forces were again attacked by Catholic youths, but the violence appeared to ebb as political tension over the weekend parade rose.

The Foreign Minister of Ireland, Britain's partner in the search for an end to the 28-year Northern Ireland conflict, appealed to the Orange Order not to insist of marching down Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road on Saturday.
Ray Burke was bitterly critical of last Sunday's Orange Order march past a Catholic housing estate along the Garvaghy Road of Portadown and of the decision to permit it.

"Our concern, of course, is that historically all of these decisions are that might is right and that is on the Orange side," Burke told reporters after attending the latest round of Northern Ireland peace talks.
"I hope Orange marchers will see there is a counter right for people not to be intimidated in their own homes," he said.

Burke was scheduled to hold talks on Wednesday with the Catholic Residents Association of the Lower Ormeau Road who have for years opposed the march past of Protestants on July 12, the most cherished date in their calendar.

His remarks were thinly-veiled criticism of Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, who was embroiled in a row over a leaked government document which said her advisers agreed weeks before the Portadown parade that it should go ahead.

Mowlam ordered an investigation into the leak and denied suggestions that shuttle talks she held with the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents were a sham because a decision to allow the parade had already been taken at the highest level.

She said the document showed only one of several options being considered by her advisers. A decision to allow the march was only announced hours before it began and after a huge security operation saturated the area to stifle dissent.
